title: Statistics - Lesson 4: Mutually Exclusive Events Assessment
description: Assessment for illustrating mutually exclusive and non-mutually exclusive events and applying probability addition rules.

questions.question: Which statement best defines mutually exclusive events?
options: Events that cannot happen at the same time in one trial
Events that always have probability 1
Events that have the same number of outcomes
Events that must be written as percentages
questions.explanation: Mutually exclusive events have no shared outcome in the same trial.

questions.question: A number cube is rolled once. Which pair is mutually exclusive?
options: Rolling an odd number and rolling an even number
Rolling an even number and rolling a number greater than 4
Rolling a number less than 5 and rolling an odd number
Rolling a 3 and rolling an odd number
questions.explanation: One number cannot be odd and even at the same time.

questions.question: Two events with different names are always mutually exclusive.
questions.explanation: Different event names can overlap. For example, a card can be both red and a heart.

questions.question: For mutually exclusive events A and B, P(A) = 1/5 and P(B) = 2/5. What is P(A or B)? Enter a fraction.
questions.explanation: Since the events are mutually exclusive, P(A or B) = 1/5 + 2/5 = 3/5.

questions.question: One card is drawn from a standard deck. Which pair is non-mutually exclusive?
options: Drawing a queen and drawing a diamond
Drawing a heart and drawing a spade
Drawing a club and drawing a diamond
Drawing a red card and drawing a black card
questions.explanation: The queen of diamonds belongs to both events, so the events overlap.

questions.question: A spinner has 10 equal sections: 4 red, 3 blue, and 3 green. What is P(red or blue)?
questions.explanation: Color sections do not overlap, so P(red or blue) = 4/10 + 3/10 = 7/10.

questions.question: If P(A and B) is greater than 0, then A and B are non-mutually exclusive.
questions.explanation: A positive intersection means at least one outcome can be in both events.

questions.question: In a survey of 50 learners, 22 like documentaries, 18 like dramas, and 7 like both. How many like documentaries or dramas?
questions.explanation: Use 22 + 18 - 7 = 33. The 7 learners in both groups are counted once.

questions.question: Using the survey in Question 8, what is the probability that a randomly selected learner likes documentaries or dramas? Enter a fraction.
questions.explanation: There are 33 favorable learners out of 50 total learners, so the probability is 33/50.

questions.question: Which formula is always safe for finding P(A or B), whether or not events overlap?
options: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B)
P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) + P(A and B)
P(A or B) = P(A) - P(B)
P(A or B) = P(A and B)
questions.explanation: The general addition rule works for all cases. If events are mutually exclusive, P(A and B) = 0.

questions.question: A learner says, "Heart and red are mutually exclusive because they are different words." Explain the mistake.
questions.correctAnswer: The events are not mutually exclusive because a heart card is also red, so the events overlap.
questions.explanation: The decision depends on shared outcomes, not on whether the event names sound different.

questions.question: A spinner has sections numbered 1 to 8. Let A = landing on an even number and B = landing on a multiple of 4. Which statement is true?
options: A and B are non-mutually exclusive because 4 and 8 are in both events.
A and B are mutually exclusive because multiples of 4 are not even.
A and B are mutually exclusive because A has more outcomes.
A and B are non-mutually exclusive because every number is a multiple of 4.
questions.explanation: A = {2, 4, 6, 8} and B = {4, 8}, so the events overlap at 4 and 8.

questions.question: If P(A) = 0.52, P(B) = 0.31, and P(A and B) = 0.18, what is P(A or B)? Enter a decimal.
Why is it important to identify the experiment before deciding whether events are mutually exclusive?
questions.correctAnswer: The experiment tells what one trial is and which outcomes can occur together; the same words may overlap in one situation but not another.
questions.explanation: Mutual exclusivity depends on the trial and sample space, so the context must be read first.

questions.question: Create a pair of mutually exclusive events and a pair of non-mutually exclusive events. Briefly explain both choices.
questions.correctAnswer: Mutually exclusive: drawing a heart and drawing a spade in one card draw, because one card has one suit. Non-mutually exclusive: drawing a queen and drawing a diamond, because the queen of diamonds is both.
questions.explanation: A full-credit response should include one no-overlap pair and one overlap pair, with the reason for each.
